commenti.body: Part of life's joy is allowing yourself to feel the full spectrum of emotion. Sadness isn't something to run away from, but just another piece of what makes us human. A movie that is willing to traffic in this end of the spectrum is also more likely to challenge other constraints a more mainstream or commercially interested film is bound by, and there is a chance for a more dynamic and complex film in general.

I get that, but what if someone spent the last few years of their life being sad all the time and wants to move forward from that? I avoid those types of films because I want to focus on being as happy as possible and not go down that path of senseless sadness, I’d rather do ratings that continue to make me happy.

Certainly differs from person to person—speaking for myself I find that sad films can be a cathartic experience since they tend to confront humane issues we all experience head-on. Still, it’s totally okay if they’re not for you. I have to be in a certain mood to put myself through something like Manchester by the Sea. Maybe someday you’ll stumble upon a feel-bad movie that clicks with you!

Can you give some examples of what a feelbad movie is? Is it something like manchester by the sea? 

Sometimes a sad movie can make someone feel good. It can be cathartic seeing a pain you’ve felt ‘heard’ and displayed by someone else going through something similar. They can also just be profound or philosophical.

There are certainly feel-bad film I have enjoyed, Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance comes to mind. But to be obsessed to the point where you are watching 4+ feel bad movies a week just doesn’t sit right with me personally.
People can't answer for your roommate but their possibly unhealthy obsession with misery porn could be an attempt to feel genuine emotion where their own experience lacks it.

if they are sad all the time then there's probably something going on that is deeper than their movie choices, frankly. And it's not senseless - in fact, many sad or scary movies help people make sense of their own fears or traumatic histories through recontextualization. Plenty of tragic moments in human history are captured or represented on film - shouldn't we honor them by remembering?

I can’t speak for your roommate since I don’t know them, but as long as they’re treating everyone else with respect and not fostering an uncomfortable environment with their behavior, I assume it’s not a big deal? Maybe reach out and ask if there’s anything going on that they want to talk about?
To name a few: Gummo, Happiness (1998), Close (2022), Martyrs (2008)

Sometimes when I'm down the sad or dark stuff is all that feels real, goes for music too.  I even know that I'm probably making it worse, but trying to force something more chipper or comedic will just seem like I'm watching through a window and left totally untouched.  Plus I'm probably not in the mood to see someone else's fun and interesting life.
